text: Edric's heir. Bailiff Crane, of the Crown. Item: forty-one things to list before Midwinter, and I shall be thorough about every one. Walk with me.
That's Crane. He counts everything twice because he's frightened of nearly everything.
Profit is an opinion. Cash is a fact. Edric never learned the difference. You will, this spring.
Now the other column, the one people prefer not to read. I brought the papers myself.
Before I stamp it, heir: do you own more than you owe, or less?
You have a head for it. That is not a compliment, heir; it is a diagnosis.
Less. Much less, and I am required to say it plainly.
The writ requires a name for the land. Item: what shall I write?
Item: {farm}. Entered on the writ, and not to be changed without a form.
That was Crane. Don't mind him: he counts everything twice because he's frightened of nearly everything.
What you own minus what you owe is yours, and yours is {eqWord}. That's why we work.
Profit is an opinion. Cash is a fact.
The far field's ripe. Harvest it (walk up, press E or tap Act) and Ashby the baker will buy.

My friend! Edric's heir! Sit, sit, no, don't sit, buy! Seed is {sc} a packet. One packet plants one plot; a plot gives {per} sacks of wheat. I wouldn't say that if it weren't true, and I would say it if it were, which is a rare quality in a salesman.
Let me buy the first three, so you can see where the coin goes.

Cash went down {three} and Inventory went up {three}: changed shape, not spent.
Seed only becomes a cost when the grain is sold.
Six more?
So you're Edric's heir. You've his chin and none of his luck, dear. I need six sacks for the ovens. Seven a sack, Cash on the nail.
Each sack cost you {cost}: {seedCost} of seed for {per} sacks, so at 7 you keep {m7} a sack. That's gross profit: {m7} out of every 7 is {p7}%, your margin.
Times are hard, dear. Would you take 6?
Work it out before you answer. Your margin at 6, in %?
I only mark up my seed 50%. Honest trade.
Your cost floor, {cost}, is the red line on the price track: sell below it and the sack costs you more than it earns. Name your price and she'll counter; you can always walk away.
That red line is your walk-away point: your best alternative, less what it costs to take it. Today it is your cost; a better buyer would raise it.
Come back when you've thought it over.
{price} it is. Ship them from your crate and I'll pay on the spot.
Before you go in: know your cost floor. And listen for when he pays.
...Edric's heir. Hm. Nine sacks. I pay... fourteen days after delivery. Same as always. Same as your uncle.
Your uncle loved Hobb, and Hobb always paid. Eventually.
Suit yourself. The offer stands till tomorrow.
The Ledger says you earned {v} today: Revenue. Look at the chest: it didn't move.
Hobb's {v} joins your Accounts receivable: everything people owe you, {arNow} in all. Hobb's part is due day {due}. Two books, and Edric only read one.
The {v} is your Accounts receivable now: Hobb owes it, due day {due}. Two books, and Edric only read one.
I... have a thing to ask. I'd rather be hit with the wheel.
The road washed out. Three weeks of flour stuck on the wrong side of a river. My customers can't pay me. So I can't pay you.
I'm asking for seven more days on the {amt} I owe you. I'll pay... eventually. I always have.
He has taken his hat off, which he does for funerals.
...Thank you. You'll... not regret it. Probably.
You just lent Hobb money: not coin, but time. A receivable is a loan you didn't price, so what did you charge him for the week?
...Fair. A man pays what he owes. I'll find it.
Half... today. Half in a week. That's... better than I asked for. You're your uncle's heir and also not.
My niece is marrying at the end of the week. A feast's worth of bread: 27 sacks. Half now to hold your place, the rest on delivery.
Ashby paid 122 today on 27 sacks you have not delivered. How much Revenue have you earned from that order so far?
Yes.
Not quite. Keep it in mind.
I can't put more on your account while you owe me this much. Pay what I'm owed first.
Seed again? Same terms: the full bill in {apDays} days, or {disc}% off if you pay within {discDays}.
On account: the full bill in {apDays} days, or {disc}% off if you pay within {discDays}.
Ezra's rate was {tvmRate}% a week when you last bought. Today it is {rate}%. Same discount, different Cash. I won't say whether that changes the answer.
A discount for paying early is an interest rate in disguise. Ezra charges {rate}% a week for Cash. I won't say which is cheaper: buy, then move the bill and see.
How many on account?
{msg}
Come in. Sit. You want coin; everyone does, eventually. My rate is {rate0}% a week. It is not a judgement, only a price. Show me your forecast first, and I shall see how much I believe it.
You owe Ezra 200 at 2.5% a week. What leaves the chest at the next pay-day for the loan?
Yes.
Not quite. Keep it in mind.
Jory walked off last night: {walkedWages} in wages and the chest couldn't find them. The crops went unwatered. The Ledger said profit. The chest said no.
Wages went out last night. Closer than the Ledger makes it look.
Practice problem 'ratio': typed, the numbers come from the player's books.
Your income statement: Revenue, minus the cost of what you sold, minus running costs. Net income {net}. Edric's always looked like this.
Your balance sheet, start and end: what you own and what you owe. Owner's equity moved by exactly your net income.
And the cash-flow statement: net income, then every place the Cash actually went. It ends at the change in Cash: {change}.

{hText}
That's what killed Edric: profit in the Ledger, the coin in other people's purses.
Edric's last page: “{page4}”
Say the number, then the reason. A claim answered with a number alone is half an answer.

The Crown's advocate will make 4 claims about this farm. Press a claim to make the advocate say more (you may learn something), then pick a card (a line from your books or a clue) and Present it to refute the claim, and 3 refuted will satisfy the court.
